Right: the spanning tree drawn with seed 7, its 15 edges in the accent color and the 9 unused grid edges dashed. Every node is reached by exactly one route, so the tree reads as a maze." width="100%"} Every spanning tree is equally likely on an unweighted graph. On a weighted graph (or with `weighted=True`), a tree is chosen with probability proportional to the product of its edge weights, so heavier edges are more likely to appear. With `multiplicative=False`, the probability is proportional to the *sum* of the edge weights instead, a much flatter distribution in which a single heavy edge can't make or break a tree. Random spanning trees are used to generate random mazes, to build sparse random backbones of a network, in Monte Carlo estimates of network reliability, and as a null model for tree-shaped data. Self-loops are never chosen. With the product distribution, edges with weight zero are never chosen either; with the sum, they can be, as long as the tree has some positive weight. Among parallel edges, each is a separate candidate. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to draw trees in proportion to the product of their edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Seed for the random number generator, for reproducible results. If `None` (default), a fresh random tree is drawn on each call. [multiplicative]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (the default), a weighted draw picks each tree with probability proportional to the product of its edge weights; if `False`, proportional to their sum. Ignored when the draw is unweighted (both are then uniform). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected graph with every node of the original (IDs, labels and attributes kept) and the `n - 1` tree edges (weights and attributes copied). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed, empty, disconnected (counting only positive-weight edges for a weighted product draw), or has a negative weight, or if every weight is zero in a sum draw. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Wilson's algorithm (1996) grows the tree from a random root. From each node not yet in the tree it runs a random walk until the walk hits the tree, erases the loops of that walk, and grafts the remaining path onto the tree. With walks that step along an edge with probability proportional to its weight, the result follows the weighted uniform spanning tree distribution exactly, $P(T) \propto \prod_{e \in T} w(e)$. The expected running time is the mean hitting time of the random walk, which is close to linear for well-connected graphs. The sum distribution $P(T) \propto \sum_{e \in T} w(e)$ is an exact mixture: pick one edge $e$ with probability proportional to $w(e)\,\tau(G / e)$, the number of trees through it times its weight, then draw a uniform spanning tree of $G$ with $e$ contracted and add $e$. By Kirchhoff's theorem $\tau(G / e) / \tau(G)$ is the effective resistance between the ends of $e$ (unit resistors), read from the inverse of the Laplacian with one row and column removed. That inverse costs $O(V^3)$ time and $O(V^2)$ memory, so sum draws suit graphs of up to a few thousand nodes. NetworkX computes the same distribution by sampling edges one at a time from contracted Laplacian determinants, which is exact but slower. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Random spanning trees of a grid are mazes: every cell is reachable from every other by exactly one route. ::: {#5623c767 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec grid = ec.Graph().add_grid_2d(4, 4) maze = grid.random_spanning_tree(seed=7) maze.count_edges(), maze.is_tree() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (15, True) ``` ::: ::: The same seed gives the same tree: ::: {#a1d8c7e6 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} again = grid.random_spanning_tree(seed=7) sorted(maze.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True)) == sorted( again.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: ::: On a weighted triangle, the tree that leaves out the light edge has weight `4 * 4 = 16` against `4 * 1 = 4` for each of the others, so it is drawn about two thirds of the time: ::: {#18b1d7e0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} tri = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) tri.add_edges([("A", "B", 4.0), ("B", "C", 4.0), ("C", "A", 1.0)]) draws = [tri.random_spanning_tree(seed=s) for s in range(3000)] sum(t.find_edge_ids("C", "A") == [] for t in draws) / 3000 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.6526666666666666 ``` ::: ::: With `multiplicative=False` the same tree weighs `4 + 4 = 8` against `4 + 1 = 5` for each of the others, so it comes up only `8 / 18`, or about 44%, of the time: ::: {#c78db921 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} draws = [tri.random_spanning_tree(seed=s, multiplicative=False) for s in range(3000)] sum(t.find_edge_ids("C", "A") == [] for t in draws) / 3000 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 0.44666666666666666 ``` ::: :::
